props.title: Presenting IT System, Web App & Developer Experience Manuals
props.subtitle: Turn documentation into presentations people actually finish — with markdown, code-based, and web-app presentation tools

what.definition: Presenting a user manual is the craft of turning written documentation for an IT system, Web App, or Developer Experience (DX) into a live, audience-shaped story — a guided walkthrough of one real task, proven in the running product, and backed by durable, findable reference material.
what.summary: Most manual presentations fail the same way: someone reads release notes aloud over an architecture diagram while the real audience — the people who must click buttons at 2am — silently disengages. This realm teaches the opposite: analyze the audience first, walk one realistic scenario end-to-end in the real UI, keep a fallback for the live demo, and hand everyone a permanent permalink to a docs site.
bullets: Audience First: end users, operators/admins, and developers each need a completely different cut of the same manual
One-Scenario Arc: hook with the user's pain, walk one persona task end-to-end, show gotchas, end with a permalink
Markdown-Native Tooling: Marp, Slidev, and reveal.js keep slides in the same Git repo as the code
Docs-as-Code Delivery: Docusaurus, MkDocs, and VitePress turn the manual into a searchable, versioned web app
Live Demo with a Safety Net: every live demo of the product ships with a pre-recorded OBS fallback clip

why.summary: A manual nobody watches or finds is a manual that doesn't exist. Teams spend weeks writing documentation, then present it in the format least likely to stick — walls of text read aloud — and then wonder why the support queue never shrinks.
why.impact: Presentations grounded in one realistic task and delivered with the right instrument (a Marp deck for a release webinar, a Swagger UI playground for API consumers, an in-app tour for self-serve onboarding) measurably cut support tickets, speed up onboarding, and make the manual self-service instead of person-service.

props.title: Audience Map — Who Is the Manual For?

categories.title: End Users
categories.subtitle: Business users & customers
categories.description: People who complete business tasks in the Web App day to day and need the manual to get unstuck in under two minutes.
categories.details: End users do not care which database backs the app. They need task-oriented walkthroughs: 'How do I export the monthly invoice report?' Show annotated screenshots of the real UI, name the exact buttons to click, and state where the permanent permalink to that page lives. Every click you skip in the slides is a support ticket you create later.
categories.analogy: A GPS navigation app — it never explains how the engine works; it says 'turn left in 200 meters' at exactly the right moment.
categories.primaryFocus: Task-oriented walkthroughs of real UI screens
inScope: Step-by-step happy paths for the top everyday tasks
Annotated screenshots with numbered callouts on exact buttons
FAQ and 'what do I do when this error appears' pages

categories.title: Operators & Admins
categories.subtitle: SRE, IT support, platform teams
categories.description: People who keep the IT system alive at 2am. They need configuration references, runbooks, and troubleshooting flows more than feature tours.
categories.details: Operators read manuals defensively: 'what breaks, how do I see it breaking, and what do I type to fix it?' Present runbooks as decision flows (symptom → diagnosis → remediation), show the actual config keys and environment variables, and demo the monitoring dashboards live. Keep every command copy-pasteable from the docs site permalink.
categories.analogy: An aircraft emergency checklist — terse, ordered, unambiguous, and identical every time the cabin altitude warning sounds.
inScope: Install/upgrade/rollback procedures with exact commands
Config file and environment variable reference tables
Alert triage flows and common failure symptom tables
outOfScope: UI walkthroughs of end-user business tasks

categories.title: Developers (DX)
categories.subtitle: Integrators & internal engineers
categories.description: People building on top of the system. For them the manual is the product: quickstarts, API references, and runnable code samples define the Developer Experience.
categories.details: Developers judge a manual the way chefs judge a kitchen — by how fast they can get something working. Lead with a five-minute quickstart that compiles, keep API references generated from the OpenAPI spec so they never drift, and make every code sample copy-pasteable and tested. In a DX presentation, live-code the integration instead of photographing it.
categories.analogy: A well-stocked workshop with labeled tools and a workbench — developers don't want a slideshow about the tools, they want to start building in ten minutes.
categories.primaryFocus: Quickstarts, API references, and copy-pasteable code samples
inScope: Getting-started quickstart that works on first try
API/SDK reference generated from OpenAPI or source annotations
Auth flows, error code tables, changelog and deprecation policy
outOfScope: Business-process background the integrator will never touch
Screenshots of UI screens the developer never renders

items.text: Stage 1 — Hook with the user's pain, not the architecture

children.text: Open with the task that currently makes people groan, e.g. 'expensing a trip takes 9 clicks today'
Never open with a microservices diagram — the audience hasn't asked for it yet

items.text: Stage 2 — Roadmap: state what they will be able to do by the end

children.text: 'By the end you can complete onboarding, refund, and export without asking support'
Follow ONE realistic persona completing ONE task end-to-end
Two shallow scenarios beat one deep one? No — one deep scenario beats two shallow ones

items.text: Stage 4 — Live demo in the running product

children.text: Drive the real UI, not screenshots pretending to be a UI
Always have a pre-recorded OBS Studio fallback clip in the presenter's pocket

items.text: Stage 5 — Gotchas: show the two or three known failure modes

children.text: Present the error message, the cause, and the documented fix side by side
End every manual presentation by pinning the permanent docs-site permalink to this slide
Tell people where the search box is — findability beats memorability

questions.question: According to the presentation arc, what is the best way to open a manual presentation?

choices.text: A microservices architecture diagram so everyone shares context
choices.explanation: The arc explicitly warns: never open with a microservices diagram — the audience hasn't asked for it yet.

choices.text: The user task that currently makes people groan, e.g. 'expensing a trip takes 9 clicks today'
choices.explanation: Correct. Stage 1 hooks with the user's pain, not the architecture.

choices.text: A full list of every feature shipped in the release
choices.explanation: Feature lists are a release notes read-aloud — the exact failure mode this realm fights. Hook with the user's pain instead.

questions.hint: Stage 1 says what NOT to open with.

questions.question: During the one-scenario walkthrough stage, how many scenarios should you cover?

choices.text: One realistic persona completing one task end-to-end
choices.explanation: Correct. One deep scenario beats two shallow ones — depth is what makes the manual stick.

choices.text: Two shallow scenarios for broader coverage
choices.explanation: The arc says the opposite: one deep scenario beats two shallow ones.

choices.text: As many as fit in the slide deck
choices.explanation: Slide count is not the constraint — depth of one end-to-end persona task is what makes Stage 3 work.

questions.hint: One bullet in Stage 3 answers with a rhetorical question.

questions.question: Which audience archetype needs config references, monitoring dashboards, and incident runbooks the most?

choices.text: End users
choices.explanation: End users need task walkthroughs of real UI screens; internal config and alert triage are explicitly out of their scope.

choices.text: Operators & admins
choices.explanation: Correct. Operators read manuals defensively: what breaks, how do I see it breaking, what do I type to fix it.

choices.text: Developers (DX)
choices.explanation: Developers want quickstarts, API references, and runnable code samples — runbooks and alert triage belong to the operators archetype.

questions.hint: Think about who is awake at 2am keeping the system alive.

questions.question: What should the final moment of a manual presentation always include?

choices.text: A teaser for the next release's roadmap
choices.explanation: Roadmap teasers belong to product pitches. Stage 6 is about making the manual findable after the talk ends.

choices.text: A recap plus the permanent docs-site permalink, and where the search box is
choices.explanation: Correct. Pin the permalink to the slide and teach people where the search box lives — findability beats memorability.

choices.text: A quiz to make sure people remember everything
choices.explanation: Memorability is not the goal — findability is. End with the permalink and the search box, not a pop quiz.

questions.hint: Stage 6 has two children, and both are about what happens after the talk.

questions.question: What safety net must a live product demo in Stage 4 always have?

choices.text: A second presenter driving a backup laptop
choices.explanation: The taught safety net is simpler and cheaper: a pre-recorded fallback clip kept ready in the presenter's pocket.

choices.text: A pre-recorded fallback clip (e.g. made with OBS Studio)
choices.explanation: Correct. Stage 4 demands a pre-recorded OBS Studio fallback clip so a frozen staging site never kills the talk.

choices.text: High-resolution screenshots to click through instead
choices.explanation: Screenshots pretending to be a UI are what Stage 4 explicitly rejects; the fallback is a pre-recorded video clip.

questions.hint: It is recorded before the presentation ever starts.

challenges.prompt: Reassemble the Six-Stage Manual Presentation Arc in the correct chronological order:

items.text: Recap + pin the permanent docs-site permalink
Hook with the user's pain, not the architecture
Gotchas: show the known failure modes with documented fixes
Live demo in the running product (fallback clip ready)
Roadmap: state what they will be able to do by the end
One-scenario walkthrough of a single persona task end-to-end

categories.title: Markdown-Native Slide Decks
categories.subtitle: Marp · Slidev · reveal.js
categories.description: Write slides as plain markdown files that compile to HTML, PDF, or PowerPoint — your deck lives in the same Git repo and pull requests as the code it presents.
categories.details: Marp turns CommonMark into slides with theme directives and exports to PDF and PPTX for the people who insist on PowerPoint. Slidev adds Vue components, live coding blocks, and presenter notes for developer audiences. reveal.js builds presentations as HTML/JS web apps with nested vertical slides, speaker notes, and Markdown fragments — a deck you can literally deploy to the same web server as the Web App.
categories.analogy: A README.md that stands up and gives a talk — version-controlled, diff-able, and reproducible like code.
categories.primaryFocus: Slides authored as code: versioned, themed, and exportable
inScope: Marp: markdown → HTML/PDF/PPTX slides with themes
Slidev: Vue-powered slides with live code editing and presenter mode
reveal.js: HTML/JS presentations that run as web apps in the browser
outOfScope: Drag-and-drop design tools with no text source of truth
Long-form hosted documentation sites (see Docs-as-Code Sites)

categories.title: Docs-as-Code Sites
categories.subtitle: Docusaurus · MkDocs Material · VitePress · mdBook
categories.description: Static site generators that turn a folder of markdown/MDX into a searchable, versioned documentation web app — the durable home the manual presentation points at.
categories.details: Docusaurus (MDX + React) gives versioned docs, a built-in search, and interactive components. MkDocs Material with mkdocs.yml is the fast, themeable workhorse for internal IT system manuals. VitePress pairs Vue-native speed with markdown for DX portals. mdBook is minimal and perfect for pure-text handbooks. All of them accept the same markdown you already wrote in the Marp deck's speaker notes, so the deck and the manual never diverge.
categories.analogy: The library the presentation was held in front of — the talk is live, but the books stay shelved, catalogued, and findable forever.
categories.primaryFocus: Durable, searchable, versioned manual delivery on the web
inScope: Docusaurus MDX docs with versioning and sidebar navigation
MkDocs Material themed sites for internal runbooks and IT manuals
VitePress and mdBook for fast markdown-native doc sites
outOfScope: Linear one-shot presentation delivery (use a deck tool)
Interactive API consoles rendered from OpenAPI (see API Reference category)

categories.title: Interactive API References & Playgrounds
categories.subtitle: Swagger UI · Redoc · Storybook
categories.description: For developer-facing manuals: render the API itself as the documentation so consumers read, try, and trust the real contract instead of a stale screenshot.
categories.details: Swagger UI renders an OpenAPI spec as an explorable, 'try it now' reference page. Redoc produces a clean three-column readable reference from the same spec. Storybook turns each UI component or SDK usage example into an interactive, isolated playground. In a DX presentation, opening the live playground IS the demo — the manual cannot be out of date because it is generated from the code.
categories.analogy: A test drive instead of a brochure about the car — the reference is the road.
categories.primaryFocus: Executable, always-current reference documentation from specs
inScope: Swagger UI interactive API consoles from OpenAPI specs
Redoc rendered API references
Storybook component & SDK example playgrounds
outOfScope: Narrative onboarding prose (put it in the docs site and link over)

categories.title: In-App & In-Code Guided Tours
categories.subtitle: Intro.js · Shepherd · VS Code Code Tour
categories.description: Teach inside the artifact itself: overlay step-by-step tours on the running Web App, or pin narrated steps to real files in the repository.
categories.details: Intro.js and Shepherd.js render highlight-and-explain overlay tours directly on your Web App screens — perfect for self-serve onboarding that never goes stale between releases. VS Code Code Tour ships .tour files in the repo that walk a developer through the manual's example project file by file, line by line. The presentation hands off into the tour instead of ending in a blank slide.
categories.analogy: A museum audio guide that starts talking when you walk into the actual room, instead of a slideshow about the museum.
categories.primaryFocus: Self-serve guided learning embedded in the product or repo
inScope: Intro.js / Shepherd overlay walkthroughs on live Web App screens
VS Code Code Tour (.tour) step files anchored to repository files
Product tour copy written in the same markdown pipeline as the manual
outOfScope: Video editing suites (see Recording & Async Demos)

categories.title: Screen Recording & Async Demos
categories.subtitle: OBS Studio · embedded clips
categories.description: Record the walkthrough once at high fidelity; reuse it as the live-demo fallback clip, the async manual for absent colleagues, and the GIF embedded in the docs page.
categories.details: OBS Studio records the real product UI with microphone narration for free and produces the pre-recorded fallback clip every Stage 4 live demo must carry. A three-minute cut of the same recording becomes the async manual for people in other time zones, and a trimmed GIF answers the question inside the docs page itself — no 'meeting recording' 47-minute graveyard.
categories.analogy: A stunt double standing by for the dangerous scene — same shot, zero risk of the live staging site freezing on camera.
categories.primaryFocus: One recording, three lives: fallback clip, async manual, docs GIF
inScope: OBS Studio screen + microphone capture of the real UI
Short clips embedded in the docs site next to the written steps
The pre-recorded fallback clip loaded before every live demo
outOfScope: Static annotated screenshots (cheaper, but a different instrument)

questions.question: You want to author slides as plain markdown in the same Git repo as the code, and still export a PPTX for stakeholders who demand PowerPoint. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Marp
choices.explanation: Correct. Marp compiles CommonMark into themed slides and exports to HTML, PDF, and PPTX.

choices.text: Redoc
choices.explanation: Redoc renders readable API references from OpenAPI specs — it does not make slide decks.

choices.text: mdBook
choices.explanation: mdBook is a minimal docs site generator for pure-text handbooks, not a slide deck exporter.

questions.hint: It is described as 'a README.md that stands up and gives a talk'.

questions.question: Your developer audience keeps getting burned by API docs that drifted from the real API. What instrument makes the reference impossible to stale?

choices.text: Longer release-notes emails
choices.explanation: Prose release notes drift exactly like screenshots do. Generate the reference from the OpenAPI spec instead.

choices.text: A Swagger UI console rendered from the OpenAPI spec
choices.explanation: Correct. Swagger UI (and Redoc) render the live contract — the reference cannot be out of date because it is generated from the code.

choices.text: High-resolution screenshots of Postman requests
choices.explanation: A screenshot of a request is still a screenshot — it goes stale the moment the API changes. Render the spec itself.

questions.hint: The manual becomes the running contract itself.

questions.question: Instead of a keynote, you want users to learn the Web App's new onboarding flow by clicking through it with highlight-and-explain overlays. Which category do you reach for?

choices.text: Intro.js or Shepherd in-app tours
choices.explanation: Correct. Intro.js and Shepherd render step-by-step overlay tours on the live product screens.

choices.text: Marp theme directives
choices.explanation: Marp makes slides; an overlay tour on live screens is the job of the In-App & In-Code Guided Tours category (Intro.js, Shepherd).

choices.text: OBS Studio
choices.explanation: OBS records video — clickable, self-serve overlay tours on running screens are Intro.js/Shepherd territory.

questions.hint: A museum audio guide inside the actual room.

questions.question: Where does the safety-net clip for a live product demo come from, and which tool makes it?

choices.text: A screen recording made with OBS Studio, reused as fallback clip, async manual, and docs GIF
choices.explanation: Correct. OBS Studio captures the real UI with narration; the same recording serves as fallback, async manual, and embedded clip.

choices.text: A second presenter with a backup laptop running reveal.js
choices.explanation: reveal.js is a presentation framework, not a recording tool. The taught safety net is a pre-recorded OBS Studio clip.

choices.text: An animated walkthrough generated by Docusaurus
choices.explanation: Docusaurus hosts docs sites; the fallback clip is a screen recording captured with OBS Studio.

questions.hint: Recorded once, it lives three lives.

questions.question: Which markdown-deck tool is specifically described as a presentation that runs as an HTML/JS web app, deployable to the same web server as the product itself?

choices.text: Marp
choices.explanation: Marp exports static decks to HTML/PDF/PPTX; the browser-native HTML/JS presentation framework in this landscape is reveal.js.

choices.text: reveal.js
choices.explanation: Correct. reveal.js builds presentations as HTML/JS web apps with nested slides and speaker notes.

choices.text: VitePress
choices.explanation: VitePress builds documentation sites from markdown; the HTML/JS presentation framework is reveal.js.

questions.hint: Its decks open in a browser tab like any other web app.

scenarios.title: Web App Manual Launch Webinar
scenarios.description: You have 30 minutes to present the user manual of a new Web App to a mixed audience of end users and operators. Forge a loadout that lands the manual without melting down on stage.

steps.title: Main Walkthrough Medium
steps.description: Stage 3-4 of the arc: how do you show the one persona task being completed?

choices.label: Pure live demo in staging
choices.description: Drive the real UI with no safety net.

pros.title: Maximum authenticity
pros.description: The audience watches the actual product, not a facsimile.

cons.title: One staging freeze from disaster
cons.description: A frozen environment mid-demo derails the whole narrative.

choices.whenToUse: Only when the staging environment has a proven track record and the network is pristine.

choices.label: Live demo + OBS pre-recorded fallback clip
choices.description: Drive the real UI, with a recorded clip cued up in the presenter's pocket.

pros.title: The show never stops
pros.description: If staging hiccups, switch to the clip mid-sentence and nobody blinks.

pros.title: Recording lives three lives
pros.description: The same clip becomes the async manual and the docs page embed.

cons.title: Extra prep time
cons.description: Recording and trimming the clip costs an hour up front.

choices.whyThisFits: Stage 4 of the arc demands a pre-recorded fallback clip; the recording amortizes into the docs site afterward.

choices.label: Static annotated screenshots
choices.description: Click through numbered callouts of the UI in the deck.

pros.title: Cannot break live
pros.description: Zero runtime risk and fastest to prepare.

cons.title: Screenshots pretending to be a UI
cons.description: The arc explicitly rejects faking the live demo.

choices.whenToUse: Acceptable for operators' runbook sections where exact config text matters more than flow.

steps.title: Slide Deck Format
steps.description: What instrument carries the hook, roadmap, and gotcha slides?

choices.label: Marp markdown deck
choices.description: Plain markdown slides in the product repo, exported to HTML/PDF/PPTX.

pros.title: Lives with the code
pros.description: The deck gets reviewed in pull requests and never contradicts the manual.

pros.title: PPTX export for stakeholders
pros.description: Satisfies the exec who only opens PowerPoint.

cons.title: Less flashy than coded decks
cons.description: Fewer interactive toys than Slidev or reveal.js.

choices.whyThisFits: A manual presentation should demonstrate the docs pipeline: the deck and the manual share one markdown source of truth.

choices.label: Slidev / reveal.js interactive deck
choices.description: Vue components, live code blocks, or a full HTML/JS web-app deck.

pros.title: Live coding dazzles developers
pros.description: Slidev's editable code blocks turn a DX talk into a workshop.

cons.title: More moving parts on stage
cons.description: Custom components and browser decks add ways to fail mid-talk.

choices.whenToUse: Developer Experience audiences where live code IS the message, and you have rehearsed twice.

choices.label: One-off clicker deck (no text source)
choices.description: Drag-and-drop slides edited directly in a presentation app.

pros.title: Familiar tooling
pros.description: Everyone's org already knows the clicker.

cons.title: Diverges from the manual
cons.description: With no markdown source, slide text rots away from the docs site.

choices.whenToUse: Last resort when policy forbids running anything but the corporate clicker.

steps.title: Take-Home Reference
steps.description: Stage 6 recap: where does the manual live after the webinar ends?

choices.label: Generated docs site permalink
choices.description: MkDocs/Docusaurus page with a permanent URL pinned on the final slide.

cons.title: One more pipeline to maintain
cons.description: The docs site needs CI to stay true.

choices.whyThisFits: The arc's final stage is recap + permalink; a generated docs site is what makes the permalink real.

choices.label: Photo of the final slide
choices.description: Audience snaps a picture of slide 32 with their phone.

cons.title: Dies in camera rolls
cons.description: No search, no updates, no follow-up links.

choices.whenToUse: Never as the only artifact — at best a complement to a permalink.

choices.label: 'It's in the repo README'
choices.description: Point developers at the raw markdown in the Git repository.

pros.title: Always current
pros.description: The source of truth is the source of truth.

cons.title: Hostile to end users and operators
cons.description: Non-developers in the room cannot use a repo README.

choices.whenToUse: Fine as an extra pointer for the DX crowd alongside the docs site.

props.title: Which Presentation Instrument Fits Your Manual?

audience.prompt: Who is the primary audience for this manual presentation?

choices.text: End users doing business tasks in the Web App
Operators & admins keeping the system alive
choices.rationale: Defensive readers need runbooks, commands, and triage flows.

choices.text: Developers integrating with the system (DX)
choices.rationale: They judge the manual by how fast the first call succeeds.

enduser-format.prompt: Will the manual be consumed live (you in the room) or async (people on their own)?

choices.text: Live webinar or workshop
choices.rationale: Live means you control the demo — but it must be rehearsed with a fallback.

choices.text: Async self-serve
choices.rationale: Async readers need findable, click-through guidance, not a recording graveyard.

leaf.recommendation: Marp markdown deck + live product demo with an OBS Studio fallback clip + in-app Intro.js tour for the next release's onboarding.
leaf.explanation: The arc demands one persona task shown in the running UI; Marp keeps the deck in the repo, the OBS clip is your stunt double, and the Intro.js tour lets users replay the flow themselves after the webinar.
tradeoffs: Prepping the fallback clip costs an hour before the talk
Marp themes need a one-time setup in the repo

leaf.recommendation: MkDocs Material or Docusaurus docs site with annotated screenshots and embedded OBS clip, plus an Intro.js/Shepherd in-app tour.
leaf.explanation: Async end users find the manual through search, so the docs site is the presentation. The embedded clip and overlay tour replace you at the keyboard.
tradeoffs: The docs site pipeline needs CI to stay truthful
In-app tours need product code changes and release coordination

leaf.recommendation: MkDocs Material runbook site (copy-pasteable commands) + reveal.js triage deck for incident reviews + Code Tour for the deploy scripts.
leaf.explanation: Operators read defensively: symptom, diagnosis, remediation. A generated runbook site keeps every command current, a browser-native reveal.js deck handles live postmortems, and Code Tour walks the deploy scripts in the repo itself.
tradeoffs: Runbook docs need ownership or they rot
Command blocks must be tested in CI to stay trustworthy

leaf.recommendation: Slidev deck with live code blocks + Swagger UI/Redoc reference rendered from the OpenAPI spec + Storybook playground + a five-minute quickstart page.
leaf.explanation: For DX, the instrument is the message: generate the reference from the contract so it cannot be stale, let the audience run code during the talk, and prove the quickstart works on first try.
tradeoffs: OpenAPI specs must be maintained as first-class code
Live coding demos need rehearsal and a recorded backup

props.title: The Release Webinar
props.intro: You are presenting the user manual of a new Web App to a mixed audience of end users and operators. Ten minutes to start; the staging environment looks 'mostly fine'. How do you run this?

start.prompt: How do you open the webinar?

choices.text: Open with the microservices architecture diagram for shared context
Open with the task people groan at: 'onboarding a new teammate takes 14 clicks today'
Read the release notes aloud so nobody misses a feature

outcome.verdict: The end users glaze over in the first two minutes; the operators were not the ones who needed the diagram either.
outcome.lesson: Stage 1 of the arc: hook with the user's pain, not the architecture. Nobody in the room asked how the system is built — they asked how to do their job.

outcome.verdict: You covered every feature. Your audience retained approximately one of them.
outcome.lesson: A release-notes read-aloud is the canonical failure mode of manual presentations. One deep persona scenario beats a shallow catalog.

demo-moment.prompt: Midway through your live demo of the onboarding flow, the staging site freezes on the big screen. What now?

choices.text: Switch seamlessly to the OBS Studio fallback clip and keep narrating
Apologize and debug the staging environment live on screen
Skip the demo and describe the flow verbally until it recovers

outcome.verdict: Nobody blinked. You finished the walkthrough, showed the gotchas, and closed on the docs-site permalink slide.
outcome.lesson: The pre-recorded fallback clip is a stunt double: same shot, zero risk. Recorded once, it lives three lives — fallback, async manual, and docs embed.

outcome.verdict: Twelve minutes of silent troubleshooting later, the demo works — and half the audience has opened their laptops to actual work.
outcome.lesson: Live debugging trades your authority for infrastructure's reliability. The fallback clip existed precisely for this moment.

outcome.verdict: Describing clicks without showing them confused end users, and the Q&A turned into a re-explanation session.
outcome.lesson: Stage 4 demands the real product on screen — or its recorded double. Pantomiming the UI is screenshots pretending to be a UI, only worse.

terms.shortDefinition: Writing documentation with the same tools and pipeline as code: markdown in Git, reviewed in pull requests, deployed by CI.
terms.detailedDefinition: Manual pages, OpenAPI specs, and tour files live in repositories, get linted and preview-built like source code, and ship through the same review discipline engineers already trust.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the only way a manual stays true after the first hotfix; documentation outside the pipeline rots within a sprint.

dialogue.user: Our manual says 'click Submit' but the button is now called 'Send'.
dialogue.aiThoughts: The docs live outside the repo, so no PR ever touched them.
dialogue.aiQuestion: What if a pull request that renames a button had to update the manual page too, or CI would flag it?

terms.shortDefinition: A permanent URL pointing at one exact page or version of the manual.
terms.detailedDefinition: The final slide of every manual presentation pins a permalink so the audience lands on the living docs page instead of a dead slide screenshot.
terms.whyItMatters: Findability beats memorability — the presentation ends, but the permalink keeps teaching for years.

terms.shortDefinition: A terse, ordered operator procedure for a specific task or incident: symptom, diagnosis, remediation.
terms.detailedDefinition: Written like an aircraft checklist so it works under stress: every command copy-pasteable, every expected output stated, no prose between steps.
terms.whyItMatters: At 2am nobody reads paragraphs; runbooks convert documentation into action.

terms.shortDefinition: A five-minute guided path that gets a developer from zero to one successful call in the real system.
terms.detailedDefinition: The DX manual's most important page: prereqs, install, auth, first request, expected output — tested on a clean machine so it works on first try.
terms.whyItMatters: Developers judge the whole product by whether the first ten minutes work; a broken quickstart is a broken product.

terms.shortDefinition: An interactive overlay (Intro.js, Shepherd) or repository walkthrough (Code Tour) that teaches by highlighting real steps in the artifact itself.
terms.detailedDefinition: Instead of slides about the product, the tour walks the user through the live UI or the actual code files, step by step, at their own pace.
terms.whyItMatters: It converts a one-time presentation into self-serve onboarding that survives every UI release.

terms.shortDefinition: A pre-recorded screen capture (OBS Studio) of the exact demo, cued up before the live presentation starts.
terms.detailedDefinition: When staging freezes on camera, the presenter switches mid-sentence to the clip and the walkthrough continues uninterrupted.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the difference between a hiccup and a cancelled launch; recorded once, the clip also becomes the async manual and docs embed.

terms.shortDefinition: A UI screenshot with numbered callouts pointing at the exact buttons and fields a task requires.
terms.detailedDefinition: The end-user manual's core unit: one screen, one task, numbered arrows naming every control in click order.
terms.whyItMatters: Every click you skip in the visuals is a support ticket you create later.

terms.shortDefinition: The cumulative feeling developers get while using a system — and its manual is often the first contact.
terms.detailedDefinition: Quickstarts, generated API references, playgrounds, error messages, and changelogs together form the DX; for many products, documentation is the product's front door.
terms.whyItMatters: A DX presentation is not 'about' the manual — it is the manual being demonstrated live, which is why the instruments (playgrounds, live code) matter so much.

challenges.template: Before choosing any tool, map your audience: {zone-1} need task walkthroughs of real UI screens, while {zone-2} read the manual defensively for runbooks and incident triage.
challenges.explanation: Correct! End users need task-oriented UI walkthroughs; operators read defensively (what breaks, how to see it, what to type). Executives were never one of the three taught archetypes.

challenges.template: The six-stage arc opens by hooking the audience with {zone-1}, proves the task in a {zone-2} of the running product, and closes by pinning the docs-site {zone-3}.
challenges.explanation: Correct! Hook with the pain (never the architecture diagram), prove one persona task in a live demo of the real product, and end on the permalink — findability beats memorability.

challenges.template: Authoring slides as markdown with {zone-1} keeps the deck in Git, rendering the OpenAPI spec with {zone-2} keeps the API reference un-stale, and recording the walkthrough with {zone-3} yields the live demo's fallback clip.
challenges.explanation: Correct! Marp compiles markdown decks that live in the repo, Swagger UI renders the API contract itself so it can never be stale, and OBS Studio records the clip that saves the live demo. Photoshop is a distractor — it appears nowhere in the realm.
